chapters.titleDe: The verb be and subject pronouns
chapters.bubble: I am, you are, she is!
comic: Stop! With she, we say is.

blocks.text: *Be* is the most important verb in English. You need it to say your name, your age, where you are from and how you feel. Almost every first conversation uses it.

blocks.title: Why is this so important?
blocks.text: An English sentence always needs a subject and a verb. In the present, *be* has three forms: *am*, *is* and *are*. Each subject pronoun has its own form. When you know them, you can make your first correct sentences: *I'm Priya. I'm from India. I'm 25.*
Subject pronouns and be
A subject pronoun stands for a person or a thing. It comes before the verb. When we speak, and in friendly messages, we usually use the short form (*I'm*, *she's*, *they're*).
*You* is for one person and for more people: *You are my teacher. You are my students.* *It* is for a thing or an animal. We also use *it* for the weather and the time: *It's cold. It's ten o'clock.*
Negatives and questions

blocks.title: Negative: be + not
blocks.text: Put *not* after *am*, *is* or *are*. The short forms are *'m not*, *isn't* and *aren't*.

head: Long form
Short form
rows: He isn't at home. / He's not at home.
We aren't late. / We're not late.

blocks.title: Questions: be comes first
blocks.text: In a question, *am*, *is* or *are* comes before the subject. A short answer repeats the verb: *Yes, I am. / No, I'm not.* (Don't use the short form at the end: *Yes, I am*, not *Yes, I'm*.)

items: Are you from Poland? Yes, I am.
Is Tom at work today? No, he isn't. He's ill.
Is it far? No, it isn't. It's only ten minutes on foot.

blocks.text: Wh- questions with be
Your age goes with *be*, not *have*: *I'm 31.* or *I'm 31 years old.* Never *I have 31 years.*
English always needs a verb. Don't leave out *be*: *She is from Brazil* or *She's from Brazil*.

blocks.title: A. Write am, is or are.

items.q: My parents ___ in Leeds this week.

blocks.title: B. Make the sentences negative. Use short forms.

items.a: The shop isn't open. / The shop's not open.
We aren't from Spain. / We're not from Spain.
They aren't at home. / They're not at home.

blocks.title: C. Write the questions and short answers.

items.a: Are you a teacher? Yes, I am.
Is Amira at work? No, she isn't.
Are your friends from London? No, they aren't.
Is it your bag? Yes, it is.

blocks.title: D. Correct the mistakes.

items.a: My sister is 18. / My sister is 18 years old.
He's from Italy. / He is from Italy.

chapters.bubble: He works, she works: don't forget the -s!
comic: My sister work in a bank.
Stop! He, she, it: the verb needs an -s.
My sister works in a bank!

blocks.text: We use the present simple for things that are always true, for habits and for things we do again and again: *I live in Bristol. She works at night. We play football on Sundays.*
The form
The verb is the same for all persons, except *he*, *she* and *it*. Here the verb gets an *-s*.
Spelling: -s, -es or -ies?

head: Verb ends in
Rule
Examples
rows: miss → misses, wash → washes, watch → watches, go → goes, do → does

blocks.text: Negatives and questions: do and does
For negatives and questions we need a helping verb: *do*, or *does* for *he*, *she* and *it*. Then the main verb has no *-s*.
Short answers
Answer a yes/no question with *do*/*does* or *don't*/*doesn't*, not with the main verb: *Do you like tea? Yes, I do.* (not *Yes, I like.*)

items: Do you like coffee? Yes, I do.
Does Zofia drive to work? No, she doesn't. She takes the bus.
Do your children speak Spanish? Yes, they do.
Where does Kwame live? He lives in Leeds.

blocks.text: Words that often go with the present simple
always · usually · often · sometimes · never · every day · on Mondays · at the weekend (US: on the weekend)
*Always*, *often*, *never* and similar words go before the main verb, but after *be*: *She often works late.* / *She is often late.*
After *does* and *doesn't*, the main verb has no *-s*. The *-s* is already in *does*.

blocks.title: A. Write the verb in the present simple.

items.q: This bus ___ (go) to the city centre.

blocks.title: B. Make the sentences negative.
C. Write questions with do or does.

items.a: Do your parents live in London?

comic: Stop! Nothing goes between like and tea.

blocks.text: English word order is quite fixed. In a normal sentence the subject comes first, then the verb, then the object. A different order can change the meaning: *The dog sees the cat.* is not the same as *The cat sees the dog.*

blocks.title: Why is this so important?
blocks.text: English has very few endings that show who does what. The place in the sentence shows it. So if you know the order, people understand you, even when you only know a few words.
The basic order: subject – verb – object
Place and time usually come at the end: first the place, then the time. A time word can also go at the very beginning.
Don't put a word between the verb and its object: *I speak English well.* (not *I speak well English*). A time word can go first: *Every morning I drink coffee at home.*
Wh- questions

blocks.title: Question word + do/does + subject + verb
blocks.text: Most questions start with a question word. Then comes *do* or *does* (or a form of *be*, or *can*), then the subject, then the main verb.

head: Question word
Asks about
Example
rows: Why do you want to learn English?
How do you get to work?
How many children do you have?

blocks.title: Yes/no questions
blocks.text: When there is no question word, the question starts with *do*/*does*, a form of *be*, or *can*.

items: Do you work here? No, I don't.
Is the station far? Yes, it is.
Can you swim? Yes, I can.

blocks.text: Who as the subject
When *who* or *what* is the subject of the question, there is no *do* or *does*: *Who lives here?* (not *Who does live here?*).

items: Who lives in this flat? Liam lives there.
Who wants a cup of tea? I do!
What happens at the end of the film?

blocks.text: A question in the present simple needs *do* or *does*. Without it, it is not a correct question.

blocks.title: A. Put the words in the correct order.

items.a: I drink coffee every morning. / Every morning I drink coffee.
Kwame plays football on Saturdays. / On Saturdays Kwame plays football.

items.q: at the station / we / at six / meet
items.a: We meet at the station at six.

blocks.title: B. Write a question. Ask about the words in brackets.

items.a: What's your name? / What is your name?
How many children does Tom have?
How does Liam go to work? / How does Liam get to work?

blocks.title: C. Write do, does, is or are.

chapters.titleDe: Nouns and articles: a, an, the
comic: Stop! For a job we need a or an.

blocks.text: English has only three articles: *a*, *an* and *the*. They don't change for men, women or things. But you need to know when to use them, and when to use no article at all.
a or an?
Use *a* or *an* with one thing that you can count. The sound decides, not the letter: *an* before a vowel sound, *a* before a consonant sound.
Use *a* or *an* for jobs: *She's a doctor. I'm an engineer.* Many languages have no article here, but English needs one.
a/an or the?
Use *a* or *an* when you talk about something for the first time, or about any one of many. Use *the* when the listener knows which one you mean.

items: I have a cat and a dog. The cat is black.
Can you close the window, please?
There's a bank near here. The bank opens at nine.

blocks.text: Plurals
Most nouns add *-s* in the plural. Some add *-es*, or change *-y* to *-ies*. A few very common nouns are irregular.

head: Rule
Singular → plural
rows: bus → buses, dish → dishes, box → boxes
man → men, woman → women, child → children, person → people, foot → feet, tooth → teeth

blocks.text: Countable and uncountable nouns
Some nouns are uncountable: they have no plural and no *a*/*an*. Use *some* or no article instead: *some water*, *I need help*.
water · milk · money · bread · rice · music · information · advice · furniture · homework
No article for things in general: *I like music. Dogs are friendly.* But *the* for a particular one: *I like the music in this film.*

blocks.wrong: Can you give me an information?
blocks.right: Can you give me some information?
blocks.text: *Information*, *advice* and *furniture* are uncountable in English. They never take *a*/*an* or *-s*.

blocks.title: A. Write a or an.
B. Write the plural.
C. Write a, an, the or – (no article).

items.q: I have a car and a bike. ___ bike is new.

blocks.text: We use the present continuous for things that are happening now, at the moment of speaking, and for things that are happening around now, for a short time: *I'm cooking dinner. Liam is staying with us this week.*
The form: am / is / are + verb-ing

blocks.title: Questions
blocks.text: Put *am*, *is* or *are* before the subject: *Are you listening? What is she doing?*
Spelling: verb + -ing

head: Rule
Examples
rows: short verb with one vowel + one consonant: double the consonant
sit → sitting, run → running, stop → stopping

blocks.text: Present simple or present continuous?
Present simple: always, usually, habits, facts. Present continuous: now, at the moment, this week.

head: Present simple
Present continuous
rows: At the moment she's working in a café.
It rains a lot in Manchester.

blocks.text: Some verbs are almost never used in the continuous, because they describe a state, not an action: *like, love, want, need, know, understand, believe, remember*. Say *I know*, not *I'm knowing*.

items: What are you doing? I'm looking for my keys.
Kwame isn't at home. He's playing football.
Are you enjoying the course? Yes, very much!
We're staying at a small hotel near the beach.
Listen! The baby is crying.

blocks.text: *Understand*, *know* and *want* are state verbs. They use the present simple, even when we mean *now*.

blocks.title: A. Write the verb in the present continuous.

items.q: I ___ (write) an email at the moment.
Mei and Tom ___ (sit) in the garden.

items.a: isn't raining / is not raining / 's not raining

items.q: We ___ (have) dinner. Can I call you back?

blocks.title: B. Present simple or present continuous? Write the correct form.

items.q: Today she ___ (walk) because the weather is nice.

blocks.title: C. Write the questions.

comic: Yesterday I goed to the cinema.
Stop! Go is irregular: go, went.
Yesterday I went to the cinema!

blocks.text: We use the past simple for finished actions and situations in the past. Often there is a past time word: *yesterday, last week, in 2019, two days ago*.
was and were
Regular verbs: -ed
Regular verbs add *-ed*. The form is the same for all persons: *I worked, she worked, they worked*.

head: Rule
Examples
rows: short verb with one vowel + one consonant: double the consonant

blocks.text: Say *-ed* as an extra syllable only after a *t* or *d* sound: *want-ed*, *need-ed*. In other verbs it is just a /t/ or /d/ sound: *worked* (one syllable), *played* (one syllable).
Irregular verbs
Many of the most common verbs are irregular. You have to learn their past forms.
Negatives and questions: did
For negatives and questions use *did* and *didn't*. After *did*, the main verb is in the base form: *I didn't go.* (not *I didn't went*).

items: Where did you go on holiday? We went to Scotland. (US: on vacation)
I called you yesterday, but you didn't answer.
Did you have a good weekend? Yes, I did, thanks.
Priya moved to London two years ago.
We weren't at home last night.

blocks.text: After *did* and *didn't*, use the base form of the verb. The past is already in *did*.

blocks.title: A. Write the verb in the past simple.

items.q: We ___ (go) to the beach on Sunday.

blocks.title: B. Make the sentences negative.
C. Write questions with did.

chapters.titleDe: Modal verbs: can, must, have to, should
chapters.bubble: I can, I must, I should!
comic: Stop! After can, we don't use to.

blocks.text: Modal verbs add a meaning to the main verb: ability, permission, obligation or advice. In one way they are easy: they never change their form.
What they mean

head: Modal
Meaning
Example
rows: I can swim. Can I sit here?
strong obligation, often the speaker's own idea
I must call my mum tonight.
obligation from a rule or from outside
I have to wear a uniform at work.
advice, the right thing to do
You don't have to come. It's not a problem.

blocks.text: The form
Modal + base form of the verb. No *to* after *can*, *must* and *should*, and no *-s* for *he*, *she* and *it*. *Have to* is different: it works like a normal verb (*she has to*, *do you have to*).
mustn't or don't have to?
*mustn't* means: it is not allowed, don't do it. *don't have to* means: it is not necessary, but you can if you want.

head: mustn't = not allowed
don't have to = not necessary
rows: You mustn't smoke in the hospital.
You don't have to bring food. We have lots.
You mustn't tell anyone. It's a secret.
It's Sunday. I don't have to get up early.

blocks.text: In positive sentences *must* and *have to* mean almost the same. In negative sentences they are very different: *You mustn't go.* (= stay!) / *You don't have to go.* (= you can stay or go).

items: Can you help me, please? Of course.
Liam can't come tonight. He has to work.
You look tired. You should go to bed early.
Do we have to pay for the course? No, it's free.
You must show your ticket on the train.

blocks.text: Modal verbs never take *-s*, and the next verb has no *to*: *she can speak*, *he should go*.

blocks.title: A. Write can, can't, should or shouldn't.

items.q: It's late. You ___ go to bed.
I ___ come to the party. I'm working that evening.
You ___ eat so much sugar. It's bad for you.
___ I open the window? It's hot in here.
You ___ drive when you are very tired.

blocks.title: B. Write mustn't or don't / doesn't have to.

items.q: You ___ cross the road when the light is red.
Tomorrow is a holiday, so I ___ work.
Tom ___ wear a suit. His office is very relaxed.

blocks.title: C. Correct the mistakes.

items.a: He must work on Saturday. / He has to work on Saturday.

items.q: She have to leave at six.
items.a: She has to leave at six.

chapters.titleDe: The future: will and going to
comic: Stop! A decision right now: use will.

blocks.text: English has several ways to talk about the future. The three most common are *going to*, *will* and the present continuous. Each one has its own job.
going to: plans and intentions
Use *am/is/are going to* + verb for something you have already decided to do. Also use it when you can see that something is going to happen: *Look at those clouds. It's going to rain.*
will: decisions now, offers, promises, predictions
Use *will* (*'ll*) + verb when you decide at the moment of speaking, for offers and promises, and for what you think about the future. The negative is *won't*.

head: Use
Example
rows: I'm thirsty. I'll have a glass of water.
That bag looks heavy. I'll carry it.
I'll call you when I get home.
I think it will be a great party. / She won't like this film.

blocks.text: Decided before? Use *going to*. Deciding now? Use *will*. *A: We need milk. B: OK, I'll get some.* / *I'm going to buy milk on the way home.* (my plan)
Present continuous for arrangements
For fixed plans with a time and a place, often with other people, we usually use the present continuous: *I'm meeting Amira at seven. We're flying to Dublin on Friday.*

items: What are you doing at the weekend? I'm visiting my parents.
I'm going to learn to drive this year.
Don't worry, I won't be late.
It's cold in here. I'll close the window.
Be careful! You're going to fall!

blocks.wrong: I will to visit my aunt.
blocks.text: After *will* comes the base form, without *to*. But after *going* we need *to*: *I'm going to visit my aunt.*

blocks.title: A. Write will ('ll) or the correct form of be going to.

items.q: A: The phone is ringing. B: OK, I ___ answer it.
We bought the tickets last week. We ___ see the show on Saturday.
Look at that sky! It ___ rain.
Sorry, I forgot. I ___ do it now.
Don't worry about the money. I ___ pay you back tomorrow, I promise.

blocks.title: B. Write the verb in the present continuous.
C. Make the sentences negative.

items.a: I won't tell her. / I will not tell her.

items.q: They're going to sell the house.
items.a: They aren't going to sell the house. / They're not going to sell the house.

chapters.bubble: Have you ever been to London?
comic: I have seen this film yesterday.
Stop! With yesterday, use the past simple.

blocks.text: The present perfect connects the past with now. We use it for experiences in our life, for past actions with a result now, and for situations that started in the past and are still true.
The form: have / has + past participle

blocks.title: The past participle
blocks.text: For regular verbs it is the same as the past simple (*worked, lived, studied*). Irregular verbs have their own form. Learn the three forms together.
*She's gone to Spain.* = she is in Spain now. *She's been to Spain.* = she went there and came back.
When do we use it?

head: Use
Typical words
Example
rows: experiences (at any time in your life)
Have you ever been to Scotland? / I've never eaten sushi.
a past action with a result now
I've lost my keys. (I can't open the door.) / She's just left.
We've lived here for five years. / I've known Liam since 2020.

blocks.text: *for* + a length of time (*for two weeks, for a long time*). *since* + a point in time (*since Monday, since 2020, since I was a child*).
Present perfect or past simple?

When you say or ask *when* something happened (*yesterday, last year, in 2019, two days ago*), use the past simple. When the time is not important, or the time is not finished (*ever, this week, today*), use the present perfect.

head: Present perfect
Past simple
rows: I've been to Paris three times.
I went to Paris last summer.
She wrote her first book in 2015.

items: Have you finished your homework yet? Yes, I've just finished it.
I've never been to Ireland, but I'd love to go.
My brother has worked in a hospital since 2021.
Where's Zofia? She's gone to the shops.
We met in 2018 and we've been friends ever since.

blocks.text: *Yesterday* is a finished time, so use the past simple. The present perfect does not go with finished time words like *yesterday*, *last week* or *ago*.

blocks.title: A. Write the verb in the present perfect.
B. Write for or since.

items.q: They've known each other ___ a long time.

blocks.title: C. Present perfect or past simple? Write the correct form.

items.q: Amira ___ (start) her new job two weeks ago.

chapters.titleDe: B1 toolkit: conditionals, relative clauses, the passive
chapters.bubble: Almost there. B1, here we come!
comic: The man which lives here is nice.
Stop! For people we say who.
The man who lives here is nice!

blocks.text: This chapter brings together three structures you need at B1: conditionals (sentences with *if*), relative clauses (*who, which, that*) and the passive. Each section shows the basic form; there is more practice online.
The first conditional: real possibilities
*If* + present simple, *will* + verb. We use it for things that can really happen in the future. The *if* part can come first or second; when it comes first, use a comma.
The second conditional: unreal or imagined situations
*If* + past simple, *would* (*'d*) + verb. We use it for situations that are not true now, or are not likely. The past form here does not mean past time.

head: if + past simple
would + verb
rows: If we lived by the sea,

blocks.text: No *will* or *would* in the *if* part: *If I have time, I'll call you.* (not *If I will have time*). *If I were you, I'd…* is the usual way to give advice.

items: If you heat ice, it melts. (always true: the zero conditional)
If the weather is nice tomorrow, we'll have a picnic.
What would you do if you won a lot of money?

blocks.text: Relative clauses: who, which, that
A relative clause tells us which person or thing we mean. Use *who* for people, *which* for things, and *that* for both.

head: Word
Used for
Example
rows: The woman who lives next door is a nurse.
The film which we saw was great.
Is this the bus that goes to the airport?

items: I have a friend who speaks five languages.
This is the phone that I bought last week.

blocks.text: The passive: is done, was done
In the passive, the person or thing that the action happens to is the subject. The form is *be* + past participle. Use *by* to say who did the action, but only when it is important.

head: Tense
Active
Passive
rows: They make cars in this factory.
Cars are made in this factory.

items: English is spoken in many countries.
The museum was opened in 1902.
This song was written by my grandfather.

blocks.wrong: If I will see her, I will tell her.
blocks.right: If I see her, I'll tell her.
blocks.text: In the *if* part of a first conditional, use the present simple, not *will*.

blocks.title: A. First conditional: write the verbs in the correct form.

items.q: If it ___ (be) sunny tomorrow, we ___ (go) to the park.

blocks.title: B. Second conditional: write the verbs in the correct form.

items.q: If I ___ (have) a car, I ___ (drive) to work.
If she ___ (live) nearer, we ___ (see) her more often.
What ___ you ___ (do) if you ___ (lose) your job?

blocks.title: C. Write who or which. (That is also correct.)

items.q: The man ___ helped me was very kind.
The book ___ I'm reading is very good.
I don't like people ___ are rude.

blocks.title: D. Make the sentences passive.

items.q: Someone cleans the office every evening.
items.a: The office is cleaned every evening.
